primary_sources.text: Boltz Swap Services are currently unavailable until further notice. We can't give an ETA as of this time, but will provide an update once we know more 🙏

Update: Boltz will stay disabled until further notice.

Our API remains available to process refunds cooperatively. In any case, unilateral refunds will work, as they do not depend on our infrastructure.

Our support team stays reachable.

To be clear: this is not a response to a single incident. Over the past months we have seen a steady rise in automated, AI-assisted probing of our infrastructure, and we have dealt with several exploits. Each was contained, but the pattern is clear: attackers now iterate faster than a team our size can find and patch. In the past few days alone we saw a drastic acceleration, and we do not believe this asymmetry will reverse. After reviewing the results of our own recent security scans, we cannot responsibly re-enable Boltz swaps, especially as we are being actively targeted by what appear to be multiple resourceful groups while we race to deploy fixes.

What we are seeing is a major paradigm shift for Bitcoin services operating on an open source stack, and it needs careful analysis. Do not expect swap services to resume shortly.

To be explicit: no user funds were ever at risk. Boltz is non-custodial by design. And as a fully bootstrapped company, the losses were ours alone.

We don't know yet how things will continue from here, but we'll keep you posted as soon as we have had the time to catch our breath and make a decision 🙏

BULL is immediately shifting our priorities to resume the ability of BULL wallet users send receive Bitcoin payments over Lightning, as well as move funds between Liquid and Bitcoin. We are evaluating multiple options and are beginning the work right now. 

Ae have been in constant contact with our very good friends at Boltz for years. We have been, and are right now, collaborating closely with their team. They are my brothers in arms and I fully support their decision to suspend their service.

Let me be clear: Bull Bitcoin is a member of the Liquid federation and can convert LBTC to BTC without a 3rs party. No BULL wallet user will have funds "stuck"  on Liquid, that I can guarantee. 

Our immediate action plans are all targeting the same goal: BULL wallet users will carry on sending and receiving Lightning payments and perform swaps between Liquid and Bitcoin. The only question are implementation details. We will figure it out. 

Until a solution is implemented, Lightning payments and Liquid <> Bitcoin swaps in the wallet will be fail without explanation. 

I will not let this situation linger. I will fix it, no matter what it takes. I will be buying my grocies with Lightning over the BULL wallet as soon as possible. 

I won't lie to you, the situation seems pretty bleak. First, the Coldcard exploit. Now, a critical piece of Lightning infrastructure goes offline. We are undoubtedly on the losing end of the Token War. Attackers have been scoring major victories. 

We are going to fight back. We will never surrender. I apologize for not giving more details. I have work to do.

The ecosystem needs bridges and the burgeoning L2 ecosystem especially so. Lightning has served the role of the connective tissue between layers for many reasons and Boltz played the lead role.

We're still looking for the next Boltz to emerge and it's not going to be us at @ambosstech (but we can help). Boltz has been an ecosystem partner (and a superlative one, at that).

Boltz and related swaps going down is a massive step backward for operability between layers.

The only real silver lining from the 2023-2024 arbitrary data frenzy was an increase in development on ways in and out of supporting layers. Boltz had been a Lightning to on-chain swap provider, but the addition of swaps with Liquid provided a revelation. A way in and out of another layer on top of Bitcoin. It was almost magical.

I've been recommending liquid-resident spending wallets essentially since they became available. I've used both the @AquaBitcoin and @BULLBITCOIN_ wallets and recommended them to people as an easier path to self-custodial Lightning. Because it's not really Lightning, it's Liquid that swaps to Lightning. Via Boltz.

At the same time, I've also been vocal about my concerns over Boltz as a single point of failure, first just theoretically, then concretely. At BTC Prague this year, Bull and Aqua wallets stopped working for a period of about 4 hours, including my own wallet. It was a concerning outage. I'm not sure it was related to their decision here, but the timing seems to indicate that it was.

I hope another provider is able to fill the void, but if there is a technical exploit to this type of swap, then I can believe that it will be difficult for someone else to offer a similar service, at least quickly. And, if this technical weakness has been there all along, then I fear that we've taken multiple steps back in terms of Layer 2 interoperability.

Of course, other technologies exist now. But I fear that we've lost a major Lightning on-and-off ramp at a time where we could have used it most.

I hope for the return of Boltz and the return of full functionality for services making use of their service. Based on their message, I'm not so optimistic, at least in the short term.

What Is Bitcoin Lightning ⚡
Bitcoin on the main chain is the base network. A new block comes about every 10 minutes on average. When many people send at once, fees go up and waiting gets longer.

Satoshi’s early idea for Bitcoin was money people could spend day to day. As the network got busier, small payments became slow and expensive. Lightning was built so Bitcoin payments can stay fast and cheap.

Lightning is a second layer on Bitcoin. It does not replace Bitcoin. It sits on top of it.

Simple example ☕
Imagine Ali wants to buy coffee every day from a shop that accepts Bitcoin.

On the main Bitcoin chain, each coffee payment can wait for blocks and pay a full network fee. That is a bad fit for a $3 coffee.

With Lightning, Ali and the coffee shop open a payment (lightening) channel together:
1) Ali locks some BTC into a special shared setup with the shop (both sides follow fixed rules; neither side can steal the locked coins alone)
2) The “two sides” are simply Ali and the shop
3) After that setup is open, Ali can pay for coffee many times in seconds, with very small fees
4) When they are done using that path, they can close the channel and settle the final totals back on main Bitcoin anytime any day.

Ali can also open a channel with his wallet provider, or an exchange, or a routing helper in the middle. The idea is the same: lock a bit of BTC with a partner once, then send many small payments without waiting for every main-chain block.

Why People Use Lightning 💳
🔶 Daily payments: coffee, tips, online checkouts
🔷 Exchange deposits and withdrawals: move BTC in and out faster and cheaper than main-chain only
🔸 Remittances: send value across borders for a small fee
🔹 Wallet moves: switch between main-chain BTC, Lightning, and other Bitcoin layers without giving up custody
🟩 Merchant checkout: shops and customers settle small sales in seconds

How Big Is Lightning Right Now 📊
🔶 Public capacity often sits near about 4,000–5,000 BTC in 2026 Peak near late December 2025 was about 5,600–5,850 BTC
🔸 Public nodes near about 17,000 (down from a peak near about 20,700 in early 2022)
🔹 Public channels near about 40,000 (down from a peak above about 80,000 in 2022)

Some researchers also put strong monthly Lightning payment volume near about $1B+ in late 2025. That shows real use. It is still a small slice of all global payments.

Several large exchanges already support Bitcoin deposits and/or withdrawals over Lightning (rules, limits, and app support can still differ by country):

✅ @binance
✅ @coinbase
✅ @krakenfx
✅ @okx

Payment apps and Bitcoin shops also matter: @Strike, @CashApp, and River-style Bitcoin platforms helped normal people send and spend this way. Size limits still apply almost everywhere. Lightning fits small and mid amounts best. Very large piles still often use the main Bitcoin chain.

What Boltz Did In This System 🔧
Boltz was a swap bridge (a tool that helps move value between main-chain BTC, Lightning, Liquid, and some stablecoin paths) without taking custody.

Wallets such as @AquaBitcoin and @BULLBITCOIN_ used that bridge so users could move between layers. @ZeusLN also runs related swap tooling. When Boltz paused, those swap buttons failed for users even though the coins in their wallets stayed under their own keys.

@Excellion said restoring Liquid and Lightning swaps is the top job for Aqua right now. @francispouliot_ said the same kind of urgent fix path for Bull Bitcoin.

Early years looked like a boom: more nodes, more channels, more “Bitcoin will be daily money” talk.

Then the public board cooled, even while real products kept shipping.

Simple reasons:
🟥 Hard for normal users: opening channels, keeping receive room ready, and fixing stuck paths is still hard. Most people want one app that works, not a home node to manage.
🟨 Money culture: a lot of demand went into holding Bitcoin, ETFs, and company treasuries, not into daily coffee spend.
🟦 Security staffing: small open Bitcoin teams now face AI-speed attackers. Boltz said that gap is a real shift, not a one-day bug.

Lightning is still Bitcoin’s main open path for fast, cheap payments after the main chain got too slow and costly for tiny spends. Big exchanges already wire it for deposits and withdrawals. Public size is still small. Private size is larger. Everyday global payments still mostly live elsewhere.
